track.legalName: Petition for Expungement or Redesignation of a Marijuana Conviction, Sentence Completed (Mont. Code Ann. § 16-12-113(5)-(10), (12))
track.mechanism: Under § 16-12-113(5)(a) a person who has COMPLETED a sentence for an act that is now permitted under Title 16, chapter 12, or that is now punishable by a lesser sentence under that chapter than the person was awarded, may petition for expungement of the conviction or for redesignation of the conviction as a misdemeanour or as a civil infraction. Section 16-12-113(5)(b) requires service on the county attorney for the county in which the petition is filed — the statute keys service to the county of FILING, not the county of prosecution. Section 16-12-113(6) directs the court to presume the petitioner satisfies the criteria unless the county attorney provides the court with a reasonable basis on which the petitioner does not; the 2021 amendment lowered that prosecutorial burden from clear and convincing evidence to providing a reasonable basis. Once the criteria are satisfied the court shall redesignate or expunge. Section 16-12-113(7) provides that unless requested by the applicant, no hearing is necessary. Section 16-12-113(8) provides that a felony conviction designated as a misdemeanour or civil infraction must be considered a misdemeanour or civil infraction for all purposes, and a misdemeanour designated as a civil infraction must be considered a civil infraction for all purposes. Section 16-12-113(9) waives no other right or remedy, § 16-12-113(10) preserves the finality of judgments in cases outside the chapter, § 16-12-113(11) applies the relief equally to juvenile cases, and § 16-12-113(12) expressly preserves the right to petition separately for misdemeanour expungement under Title 46, chapter 18, part 11. Procedure is governed by the Temporary Rules adopted by Montana Supreme Court order AF 22-0129, filed 15 March 2022, and the Office of the Court Administrator publishes Form B with a Certificate of Service and a Proposed Order. Enacted as Sec. 36, I.M. No. 190, effective 1 January 2021, amended by Sec. 48, Ch. 576, L. 2021.
exclusions: Acts that remain criminal at the same level under Title 16, chapter 12. The whole test is whether the conduct is now permitted or is now punishable by a lesser sentence.
Convictions from out-of-state, federal or Tribal courts.
A participant who is still serving the sentence, who belongs on the currently-serving track under § 16-12-113(1) rather than this one.
Anything outside Title 16, chapter 12: § 16-12-113(10) preserves the finality of judgments in those cases.

units.label: MMRTA Form B petition in the sentencing court, with certificate of service and proposed order
units.description: The court stage. One complete set per conviction — MMRTA Form B, the OCA Certificate of Service and the OCA Proposed Order — filed in the court that sentenced the participant, with a copy of the participant's Montana Department of Justice criminal record attached, which Form B marks required. The Office of the Court Administrator publishes the whole set under Montana Supreme Court authority in AF 22-0129, the forms carry no use restriction, and they encode the statutory offence list, the required attachments, the § 16-12-113(7) hearing election and the § 16-12-113(5)(b) service requirement. LegalEase completes the caption for the correct court level, the participant's identity and case facts, the offence selection the participant makes from the enumerated list, and the conviction date. It does not complete the narrative explaining why the conviction is eligible, and it does not choose among expungement, misdemeanour redesignation and civil-infraction redesignation. The Certificate of Service names the county attorney for the county in which the petition is filed. The Proposed Order leaves every judicial finding and the signature blank.

units.label: DOJ CRISS submission after an expungement order
units.description: The Department of Justice stage, and a separate legal unit with its own destination and its own participant submission: the court order does not itself clear the DOJ criminal history record. LegalEase completes the participant-owned fields of the CRISS Expungement/Removal Request Form and supplies the mailing checklist and verification steps; the participant encloses the original or certified court judgment and the court order of expungement and mails them to CRISS. This unit applies where the outcome is EXPUNGEMENT. Where the participant instead obtains redesignation as a misdemeanour or as a civil infraction, the conviction is not expunged and there is no DOJ deletion stage to complete, so the unit does not apply and the packet says so rather than sending a request that will be refused. No FD-258 fingerprint card is required for the marijuana request type, unlike the misdemeanour expungement track.

track.venue: Whichever court sentenced the participant. Form B provides three caption options — Montana Judicial District Court by county, Justice Court of a county, and Municipal or City Court — and recites that venue is proper because it is the court in which the participant was sentenced. This is a materially different venue rule from the misdemeanour expungement track, which always goes to District Court.

selfHelpBoundaries: Any uncertainty about whether the historical conduct is now permitted or is now punishable by a lesser sentence under Title 16, chapter 12.
Any offence not on the OCA form's enumerated list, which forces the free-text specify-offence line.

The offence-mapping question is a self-help boundary: whether the historical conduct is now permitted, or is now punishable by a lesser sentence, under Title 16, chapter 12 requires mapping decades-old charging language and quantities against the current chapter, and it is the central legal question of the track. LegalEase presents the enumerated statutory list and the participant selects; the free-text specify-offence path is an attorney handoff.

County attorney opposition within the twenty-one-day window, and any hearing the participant elects, are post-generation handoff. § 16-12-113(6) requires the county attorney to give the court a reasonable basis on which the petitioner does not satisfy the criteria.

packetInstructions: Montana's three words are not interchangeable and participant copy must keep them apart. Expungement under § 46-18-1103(1) means to permanently destroy, delete or erase a record from the criminal history record information system maintained by the Department of Justice. What happens at the courts, law-enforcement agencies and prosecutors' offices is sealing, not destruction (§ 46-18-1110(2)(a)). Removal is the DOJ term for deleting a non-conviction record. Redesignation and resentencing are MMRTA outcomes and are neither.

The court order is not the end in Montana. Under § 46-18-1110(2)(b) the person whose records are being expunged, not the court and not the clerk, must send the order to the arresting agency, the prosecutor, the clerk and the Department of Justice, together with fingerprints and the DOJ form; § 46-18-204(2) holds the same pattern for deferred dismissals; and the OCA MMRTA instructions say the same. A Montana packet that stops at a signed court order leaves the conviction sitting on the participant's background check.

The two-portal court search is a required participant step, not a suggestion: one search of the Montana Public Access Portal for District Courts and one for Courts of Limited Jurisdiction. Montana has no centralised court records system, and some misdemeanour convictions do not appear on the CRISS background check at all.

One complete form set per conviction, never a consolidated petition. The OCA instructions require a separate form for each conviction even where the convictions occurred at the same time. This is the opposite of the misdemeanour expungement track, where one petition covers the whole record, and the rules engine must not generalise across the two.

Fee lookup must branch on court level and must not default to the District Court figure. The $120 civil commencement fee is the District Court schedule; Justice, Municipal and City Court fees are different and were not resolved. The OCA instructions confirm the participant is responsible for filing fees and other costs.

The OCA instructions state expressly that the participant must follow all applicable filing rules including local filing rules, and route the participant to the Court Locator for local rules and contact information. This is an acknowledged local-practice dependency and is built as a required lookup step.

§ 16-12-113(12) is express: petitioning under that section does not make a person ineligible to petition for misdemeanour expungement under Title 46, chapter 18, part 11. A participant can use both, and the eligibility engine must present them as complementary rather than alternative.
Note that § 16-12-113(5)(b) keys service to the county in which the petition is filed, not the county of prosecution.
participantQuestions: LegalEase does not choose among expungement, redesignation as a misdemeanour, and redesignation as a civil infraction. These are materially different outcomes with different consequences, the form requires the participant to choose, and the election is the participant's alone. Any analysis of which outcome is better is legal advice and triggers handoff.
scopeRestrictions: The Misdemeanor Expungement in Montana packet (ER-100, ER-200 and the Statement of Inability to Pay Court Costs and Fees) and the Dismissal After Completing a Deferred Sentence packet (DS-100 and DS-200) are stamped '© 2025 Montana Legal Services Association and Montana Supreme Court Access to Justice Commission. This form may be used for non-commercial purposes only.' Expungement.ai is a paid product, so reproducing or distributing them inside a packet is a commercial use. They are drafting references only: never generated, never relabelled, never converted, never lightly rewritten, never runtime-selectable and never generation_allowed. The restriction changes source use, not the existence of the mechanism.

No participant-facing statement that the participant may deny the conviction after expungement, after a deferred dismissal, or after a non-conviction removal. No Montana perjury shield or restoration-to-prior-status provision was located in any of the three statutes, and whether a cleared record may lawfully be denied is a hard self-help stop.

releaseBlockers.question: Which CRISS Expungement/Removal Request Form version the Department of Justice enforces in practice, and what the current required attachment set is. The 2023 PDF and the 29 April 2024 DOCX disagree: the 2023 version requires valid photo identification for the Non-Conviction Removal and Deferred Imposition request types and requires the 'Original Court Order' for misdemeanour expungement, while the 2024 version drops the photo-ID requirement, requires the 'Original Court Judgement' instead, and adds 'Deferred Prosecution' to the fourth request type. Master Library Edition 1.1 retains the 2024 version as the supporting-process asset and does not retain the 2023 PDF. The 2024 version is used for legal design and the 2023 version is preserved as history only; the packet includes photo identification by default, which is the fail-closed reading, and asks for a certified copy of the judgment.

provenance.sourceStatement: The 2023 and 2024 CRISS form versions disagree on required attachments. The 2023 PDF requires valid photo identification for the Non-Conviction Removal and Deferred Imposition request types and requires the "Original Court Order" for misdemeanor expungement. Unresolved which set CRISS enforces in practice.

releaseBlockers.question: Master Library Edition 1.1 retains the CRISS Expungement/Removal Request Form as a SUPPORTING_PROCESS asset with document role SUPPORTING_FORM, not as a packet form. The authority gate treats a supporting-process asset as one that cannot back an official_pdf_fill component, so every Montana component that maps to it is recorded as an authority role mismatch. The classification is the issue, not the mechanism: the form is a genuine Department of Justice agency form, it carries no use restriction, § 46-18-1110(2)(b) and § 46-18-204(2) both refer to a form prepared by the department of justice, and it is the required and only vehicle for the DOJ stage of four Montana tracks and for the whole of the non-conviction removal track. The mapping is retained rather than dropped, because pointing at the retained asset is truthful and preserves traceability, and the asset-class question is carried here as an explicit release blocker and a proposed Edition 1.2 reclassification. Edition 1.1 is not modified.

releaseBlockers.question: Master Library Edition 1.1 gives the OCA MMRTA Proposed Order and the OCA MMRTA Certificate of Service the SAME document ID, MT-OCA-MMRTA, distinguished only by document role, ORDER against SERVICE. They are two different binaries with two different SHA-256 values, so a component that names MT-OCA-MMRTA matches two retained assets carrying conflicting hashes and the authority gate records an authority hash conflict. This is an Edition 1.1 source-identity problem rather than a defect in the Montana legal design: both forms exist, both are published by the Office of the Court Administrator, both are retained, and both are correctly placed in the packet. Each needs its own document ID in a successor edition before either component can be resolver-selectable. The mappings are retained and the tracks stay authority-gated.

legalDesignLimitations.statement: Montana's three words are not interchangeable and participant copy must keep them apart. Expungement under § 46-18-1103(1) means to permanently destroy, delete or erase a record from the criminal history record information system maintained by the Department of Justice. What happens at the courts, law-enforcement agencies and prosecutors' offices is sealing, not destruction (§ 46-18-1110(2)(a)). Removal is the DOJ term for deleting a non-conviction record. Redesignation and resentencing are MMRTA outcomes and are neither.

provenance.sourceStatement: Correct jurisdiction-specific terminology: "Expungement." Montana defines the word narrowly at § 46-18-1103(1): to permanently destroy, delete, or erase a record of an offense from the criminal history record information system maintained by the Department of Justice. What happens at the courts, law enforcement agencies, and prosecutors' offices is sealing, not destruction (§ 46-18-1110(2)(a)). Do not use the two words interchangeably in participant copy.

legalDesignLimitations.statement: The Misdemeanor Expungement in Montana packet (ER-100, ER-200 and the Statement of Inability to Pay Court Costs and Fees) and the Dismissal After Completing a Deferred Sentence packet (DS-100 and DS-200) are stamped '© 2025 Montana Legal Services Association and Montana Supreme Court Access to Justice Commission. This form may be used for non-commercial purposes only.' Expungement.ai is a paid product, so reproducing or distributing them inside a packet is a commercial use. They are drafting references only: never generated, never relabelled, never converted, never lightly rewritten, never runtime-selectable and never generation_allowed. The restriction changes source use, not the existence of the mechanism.

provenance.sourceHeading: READ THIS FIRST: FOUR FINDINGS THAT CHANGE THE MONTANA BUILD
provenance.sourceStatement: The best Montana misdemeanor forms carry a non-commercial-use restriction. LegalEase cannot ship them. Every page of the Misdemeanor Expungement in Montana packet (forms ER-100 and ER-200 plus the Statement of Inability to Pay Court Costs and Fees) is stamped: copyright 2025 Montana Legal Services Association and Montana Supreme Court Access to Justice Commission, "This form may be used for non-commercial purposes only."

legalDesignLimitations.statement: The court order is not the end in Montana. Under § 46-18-1110(2)(b) the person whose records are being expunged, not the court and not the clerk, must send the order to the arresting agency, the prosecutor, the clerk and the Department of Justice, together with fingerprints and the DOJ form; § 46-18-204(2) holds the same pattern for deferred dismissals; and the OCA MMRTA instructions say the same. A Montana packet that stops at a signed court order leaves the conviction sitting on the participant's background check.

provenance.sourceHeading: READ THIS FIRST: FOUR FINDINGS THAT CHANGE THE MONTANA BUILD
provenance.sourceStatement: The court order is not the end in Montana. Every conviction track needs a second, participant-initiated submission to DOJ CRISS. Under § 46-18-1110(2)(b) the person whose records are being expunged, not the court and not the clerk, must send the order to the arresting agency, the prosecutor, the clerk, and the Department of Justice, together with fingerprints and the DOJ form.

legalDesignLimitations.statement: The two-portal court search is a required participant step, not a suggestion: one search of the Montana Public Access Portal for District Courts and one for Courts of Limited Jurisdiction. Montana has no centralised court records system, and some misdemeanour convictions do not appear on the CRISS background check at all.

provenance.sourceStatement: The two-portal court search (District Courts and Courts of Limited Jurisdiction) is a required participant step, not a suggestion.

legalDesignLimitations.statement: No participant-facing statement that the participant may deny the conviction after expungement, after a deferred dismissal, or after a non-conviction removal. No Montana perjury shield or restoration-to-prior-status provision was located in any of the three statutes, and whether a cleared record may lawfully be denied is a hard self-help stop.

provenance.sourceStatement: No participant-facing statement that the participant may deny the conviction after expungement.

legalDesignLimitations.statement: LegalEase does not choose among expungement, redesignation as a misdemeanour, and redesignation as a civil infraction. These are materially different outcomes with different consequences, the form requires the participant to choose, and the election is the participant's alone. Any analysis of which outcome is better is legal advice and triggers handoff.

provenance.sourceHeading: Questions that require individualized legal judgment and cannot safely be automated
provenance.sourceStatement: Whether the participant should ask for expungement, redesignation as a misdemeanor, or redesignation as a civil infraction. These are materially different outcomes and Form B requires the participant to choose.

legalDesignLimitations.statement: The offence-mapping question is a self-help boundary: whether the historical conduct is now permitted, or is now punishable by a lesser sentence, under Title 16, chapter 12 requires mapping decades-old charging language and quantities against the current chapter, and it is the central legal question of the track. LegalEase presents the enumerated statutory list and the participant selects; the free-text specify-offence path is an attorney handoff.

provenance.sourceStatement: The offense-mapping question is a self-help boundary; LegalEase presents the enumerated statutory list and the participant selects, with an attorney handoff on the free-text path.

legalDesignLimitations.statement: One complete form set per conviction, never a consolidated petition. The OCA instructions require a separate form for each conviction even where the convictions occurred at the same time. This is the opposite of the misdemeanour expungement track, where one petition covers the whole record, and the rules engine must not generalise across the two.

provenance.sourceStatement: One complete form set per conviction, never a consolidated petition.

legalDesignLimitations.statement: Fee lookup must branch on court level and must not default to the District Court figure. The $120 civil commencement fee is the District Court schedule; Justice, Municipal and City Court fees are different and were not resolved. The OCA instructions confirm the participant is responsible for filing fees and other costs.

provenance.sourceStatement: Fee lookup must branch on court level, not default to the District Court figure.

legalDesignLimitations.statement: The OCA instructions state expressly that the participant must follow all applicable filing rules including local filing rules, and route the participant to the Court Locator for local rules and contact information. This is an acknowledged local-practice dependency and is built as a required lookup step.

legalDesignLimitations.statement: § 16-12-113(12) is express: petitioning under that section does not make a person ineligible to petition for misdemeanour expungement under Title 46, chapter 18, part 11. A participant can use both, and the eligibility engine must present them as complementary rather than alternative.

provenance.sourceStatement: Interaction with Track 1: § 16-12-113(12) is express. legalDesignLimitations.statement: County attorney opposition within the twenty-one-day window, and any hearing the participant elects, are post-generation handoff. § 16-12-113(6) requires the county attorney to give the court a reasonable basis on which the petitioner does not satisfy the criteria.

provenance.sourceStatement: Response or objection period: 21 days for the county attorney to respond in opposition, per the OCA instructions.

legalDesignLimitations.statement: Note that § 16-12-113(5)(b) keys service to the county in which the petition is filed, not the county of prosecution.

provenance.sourceStatement: Notice recipients: The county attorney for the county in which the petition is filed (§ 16-12-113(5)(b)). Note the statute keys service to the county of filing, not the county of prosecution.
